title: Seeing in Silhouette
sub: Grades 5–8 · Art · Aaron Douglas and the visual language of the Harlem Renaissance
objective: Students will analyze Aaron Douglas’s distinctive visual style — flat geometric silhouettes, layered concentric circles, African design influences, and deliberate use of color to evoke emotion and narrative. They will understand how formal art choices carry meaning and argument, and respond through their own silhouette composition or analytical writing.
materials: Printed or projected Aaron Douglas images — the handouts name each work; ideal to also display large-format
For studio activity: black card or paper, scissors, colored backgrounds (construction paper or watercolor wash on white card); alternatively, pencil and colored pencils for composition sketches
connection: **Option 1 — Visit the exhibition:** bring your class to experience the phonograph, the Great Migration Map, the Jazz Lab, and more. Ask your librarian to arrange a visit.
**Option 2 — Virtual visit:** online at the address below.

steps.title: What do you see?
script: Project *Song of the Towers* (1934) without any introduction. Ask students to write three observations in 60 seconds — not interpretations, just observations.
*“Don’t tell me what it means yet. Tell me what you see. Be specific — shapes, colors, positions of figures, what’s in the background, what’s in the foreground.”*

Take 5–6 responses. Then: *“This painting was made in 1934 by Aaron Douglas. He was the leading visual artist of the Harlem Renaissance. Today we’re going to figure out how he made it work — and why.”*

steps.title: Five signature techniques
script: Walk through Douglas’s five signature techniques:
**Flat silhouettes:** figures rendered without facial features — universal, archetypal, collective rather than individual
**Concentric circles:** light radiating outward from a center — spiritual energy, sound waves, divine presence
**African geometric pattern:** influenced by Egyptian hieroglyphics and West African textile design — a deliberate reclamation of African visual heritage
**Limited, symbolic color palette:** each painting uses 3–5 colors with specific emotional associations
**Layered transparency:** figures overlap in semi-transparent layers — collective history, multiple times existing simultaneously

steps.title: Every choice was deliberate
script: *“Douglas was trained in European art — he knew exactly what ‘mainstream’ painting looked like. He chose not to paint that way. Every choice he made was deliberate: the silhouettes say ‘this is everyone, not one person.’ The concentric circles say ‘there is spiritual power here.’ The African patterns say ‘we come from somewhere ancient and magnificent.’ His paintings were arguments made in color and shape.”*

steps.title: Choose a handout

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Complete a structured visual analysis of *Song of the Towers* using five guided questions. Then create a simple silhouette figure in the style of Douglas — black on colored background, one symbol added.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Analyze two Douglas works — compare how he uses the same techniques in different emotional contexts. Create a silhouette composition with at least three figures and a symbolic background. Write a 3-sentence artist statement.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Full formal analysis of three works across all five technique dimensions. Write a 2-paragraph critical interpretation arguing what Douglas’s visual choices communicate about Black identity and history. Optional studio: respond in your own silhouette composition with written rationale.

steps.purpose: Analyze and make in Douglas’s visual language, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. You can switch at any time.
